slides: Welcome back, and now a new topic, counting possibilities.

slides.say: In these questions we count how many ways there are to arrange something, or to choose something. We always count according to the data in the question.

slides: The math name for this is combinatorics. It comes from the word combination, and a combination is simply one possibility.
Counting questions come up in almost every exam. So let's learn them step by step.

slides.say: Before we count anything, we decide what counts as a different result.
Two friends, Dan and Mia, stand in a row. Dan, then Mia, is one row.
at: Dan, then Mia, is one row

slides.say: Mia, then Dan, is another row. We swapped them, so the order changed. So here we have two different rows.
at: Mia, then Dan, is another row

slides.say: Now we pick the same two friends for a team. Dan and Mia is the same team as Mia and Dan. The order doesn't matter in a team.
at: Dan and Mia is the same team

slides.say: And in a code, one two and two one are different codes, because the digits are in different places.
at: one two and two one are different codes

slides.say: So in every question, first ask yourself one thing. Does the order matter? We'll come back to this question all through the topic.
One more thing before we start. Some questions with the same kind of story ask at most how many, or at least how many.
Those are not counting questions. They are the extreme questions from topic twenty-one. Remember, we push to the extreme, and we give the others as little as possible.

slides: So when you see at most or at least, use the topic twenty-one way. Everything else in this topic, we count.

slides.say: The first way to count is the simplest one. We just write the options, check which ones fit, and count them. This is trial and error.
Let's see an example. How many two-digit numbers can we make from the digits two, four and seven, if the tens digit is smaller than the units digit?
at: How many two-digit numbers can we make

slides.say: We list them in order, with the smallest tens digit first. The tens digit is two. Then the units digit can be four, so twenty-four.
Or the units digit can be seven, so twenty-seven. Both units digits are bigger than two, so both numbers fit.
Now the tens digit is four. The units digit must be bigger than four, so only seven. That's forty-seven.
And the tens digit seven? No digit here is bigger than seven. So seventy-two, for example, doesn't fit.
So there are three numbers. What did we do? We counted, and we checked.
Now another example. In how many ways can we write eight as a sum of two whole numbers bigger than zero? The order doesn't matter here.
at: In how many ways can we write eight

slides.say: Again we list in order. We start with the smallest first number, one. One plus seven.
Then two plus six, and three plus five.
Then four plus four. Four plus four is eight, so it fits too.
What about five plus three? It's the same as three plus five, and the order doesn't matter. So we stop here.
So there are four ways.
That's why we list in order, smallest first. Nothing is missed, and nothing is counted twice.

slides: Listing works well when the list is short. When the list is long, we need a faster way. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
